MUJAHID:v2p651#2/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p651#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
MUJAHID:v2p651#2/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets the locations of the stars as the Qur'an's points of descent: the Qur'an descended all at once to the lowest heaven, then came to the Prophet in separate portions.

MUJAHID:v2p651#2/r2.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p651#2/r2.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p651#2/r2.claim: Mujahid says the locations are the stars in the sky, including their risings and settings.

MUQATIL:56:74-82/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:56:74-82/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:56:74-82/r2.claim: The locations of the stars refer to the Quran's descent, all of it, on the Night of Power from the Preserved Tablet in the seventh heaven to the lowest heaven and the angelic scribes.

MUQATIL:56:74-82/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:56:74-82/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:56:74-82/r3.claim: The scribes are angels, as in the description of noble, righteous scribes in 80:15-16.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p273#2/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p273#2/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p273#2/r1.claim: Qatada explains the stations of the stars as their positions.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p273#2/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p273#2/r2.speaker: الكلبي
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p273#2/r2.claim: Al-Kalbi says the oath refers to the Quran as it descended in successive portions.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p451#6/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p451#6/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p451#6/r1.claim: The locations of the stars are the positions of the Qur'an's stars when its verses were revealed.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p451#6/r2.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p451#6/r2.speaker: أبو عبيدة
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p451#6/r2.claim: Abū ʿUbayda instead means the setting places of stars in the west.

TAB-FULL:v22p359/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p359/r1.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
TAB-FULL:v22p359/r1.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr reads the opening as an oath: “I swear.”

TAB-FULL:v22p359/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p359/r2.speaker: بعض أهل العربية
TAB-FULL:v22p359/r2.claim: Some Arab grammarians take “no” as rejecting the opponents' claim before beginning a fresh oath.

TAB-FULL:v22p359/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p359/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v22p359/r3.claim: One interpretation takes the stars' “positions” as the places of the Qur'an's revelation, since it descended in portions over time.

TAB-FULL:v22p359/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p359/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v22p359/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says the Qur'an descended on the Night of Decree to the lowest heaven all at once, was then divided over the years, and recites this verse as evidence.

TAB-FULL:v22p359/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p359/r5.speaker: عكرمة
TAB-FULL:v22p359/r5.claim: ʿIkrima says the Qur'an was revealed in star-like portions of three, four, or five verses.

TAB-FULL:v22p359/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p359/r6.speaker: عكرمة
TAB-FULL:v22p359/r6.claim: A report from ʿIkrima says the Qur'an was revealed together and placed at the stars' positions, then Gabriel brought it down as chapters; it was all revealed on the Night of Decree.

TAB-FULL:v22p359/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p359/r7.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v22p359/r7.claim: Mujahid glosses the stars' positions as the Qur'an's decisive or firmly established portions.

TAB-FULL:v22p359/r9.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p359/r9.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v22p359/r9.claim: Another group interprets the phrase as the stars' setting places.

TAB-FULL:v22p361/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p361/r1.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v22p361/r1.claim: Mujahid locates the stars in the sky and glosses their mawāqiʿ as their risings and settings.

TAB-FULL:v22p361/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p361/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v22p361/r2.claim: Qatāda interprets the stars’ mawāqiʿ as their settings.

TAB-FULL:v22p361/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p361/r3.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v22p361/r3.claim: Qatāda also reports the interpretation that the oath is by the stars’ stations.

TAB-FULL:v22p361/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p361/r4.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v22p361/r4.claim: Al-Hasan interprets the sites as the stars’ darkening and scattering on Judgment Day.

TAB-FULL:v22p361/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p361/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v22p361/r5.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers the stars’ setting and disappearance in the sky: mawqiʿ is the place or time of falling, its most evident sense here.

TAB-FULL:v22p361/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p361/r6.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v22p361/r6.claim: Kufan readers mostly read the singular mawqiʿ; most Medinan and Basran readers and some Kufans read the plural mawāqiʿ. Both are recognized and equivalent.

ZAJJAJ:v5p115/r6.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p115/r6.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p115/r6.claim: “No, I swear” means “I swear”: lā strengthens the oath, as lā in li-allā yaʿlama means “so that the People of the Book may know.”

ZAJJAJ:v5p115/r7.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p115/r7.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p115/r7.claim: The stations of the stars are their setting places; compare the oath by the Lord of the easts and wests.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3334#4/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3334#4/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3334#4/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the stars' settings as the Quran and says the Quran is the great oath meant by the following clause.

NAHHAS:v4p341/r13.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v4p341/r13.speaker: ابن عباس
NAHHAS:v4p341/r13.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās takes the stars' stations as the descent of the Qur'an; al-Farrāʾ supports this from the next verse.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p262#2/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p262#2/r1.speaker: أبو عبيدة
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p262#2/r1.claim: Abū ʿUbaydah takes فلا أقسم as فأقسم and مواقع النجوم as their settings, where the stars disappear.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p262#2/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p262#2/r2.speaker: قيل
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p262#2/r2.claim: Another interpretation makes the مواقع the successive places where the Qur'an descended to the Prophet; the phrase can also connect to the oath by the star in 53:1.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p262#2/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p262#2/r3.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p262#2/r3.claim: A verbal noun or generic noun may be singular for one kind and plural when its instances differ; this explains singular موقع versus plural مواقع.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p262#2/r4.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p262#2/r4.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p262#2/r4.claim: In the cited verse, مواقع الطير means multiple places rather than a verbal noun, so its plural reflects the several bird perches.

SULAMI:v2p302/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p302/r1.speaker: ابن عطاء
SULAMI:v2p302/r1.claim: The appointed stations are what appears on the Prophet's inner secret of divine lights and added realization, including special nearness that he was not commanded to disclose.

THALABI:v9p217/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v9p217/r10.speaker: author
THALABI:v9p217/r10.claim: The sites of the stars are the locations where Quranic passages descended as its verses came down and spread on the Resurrection Day.

THALABI:v9p217/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v9p217/r8.speaker: author
THALABI:v9p217/r8.claim: Most commentators take 'I do swear' as an oath with an extra la; the verified reading by Isa ibn Umar supports that construction.

THALABI:v9p217/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v9p217/r9.speaker: بعض أهل العربية
THALABI:v9p217/r9.claim: Some Arab grammarians take la as a denial of the opponents' claim, followed by a newly begun oath over the sites of the stars.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r1.speaker: الضحاك
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r1.claim: One view denies God swears by created things; the phrase opens speech, not an oath.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r10.speaker: ابن مسعود
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r10.claim: Al-Farra relates that the stations are the decisive Qur'anic verses.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r2.claim: Another view allows the Creator to swear by creatures to honor them.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r3.claim: On that view, lā is extra and the phrase means I swear.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r4.claim: Alternatively, lā answers what preceded: do not deny God's blessings and proofs; the oath then begins anew.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r5.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r5.claim: The stations are stars' risings and settings.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r6.speaker: الحسن
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r6.claim: They may be stars scattering and extinguishing on Judgment Day.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r8.speaker: الضحاك
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r8.claim: They may be the anwaʾ to which pre-Islamic Arabs attributed rain; this reading negates swearing by them.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r9.speaker: ابن عباس والسدي
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p462/r9.claim: They are stages of Qur'anic revelation from the Preserved Tablet to heavenly scribes and through Gabriel to Muhammad over twenty years.

QUSHAYRI:v3p279/r4.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p279/r4.speaker: قيل
QUSHAYRI:v3p279/r4.claim: The oath by the stars' positions can refer to stars in the sky or the Quran's successive descents upon the Prophet's heart.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r1.speaker: أكثر أهل العلم
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r1.claim: Most scholars treat لا as an extra particle, so the phrase means I swear; such added لا is common in speech and revelation.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r10.speaker: الحسن
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r10.claim: Al-Hasan interprets the sites as stars scattering and falling apart; this fits the plural reading as each star has its own fall.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r2.speaker: أهل المعاني
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r2.claim: The scholars of meaning take لا as a rejection of the claim that the Quran is magic, poetry, or divination, followed by a new oath that it is noble scripture; compare 4:65.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r3.claim: The author notes the singular reading موقع alongside the plural مواقع.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r4.speaker: أبو عبيد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r4.claim: Abu Ubayd prefers the plural, taking the locations as places where Quran verses were revealed in installments; he says the plural also suits star settings.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r5.speaker: المبرد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r5.claim: Al-Mubarrad says the singular موقع is a verbal noun that can denote a little or much, one or many.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r6.speaker: أبو علي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r6.claim: Abu Ali says singular fits when the sites are treated as one generic kind, whereas plural fits when their kinds differ; he compares plural and singular sound in 31:19.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r7.claim: The cited poet's phrase مواقع الطير means the places where birds alight on a rock, so there the word is a plural of locations rather than a verbal noun.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r8.claim: Ibn Abbas, through Ata, identifies the sites of the stars as the descent of the Quran; al-Kalbi, Muqatil, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, and Qatada agree.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r9.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p256#2/r9.claim: Other exegetes, including Abu Ubayd, identify the sites as star settings or disappearances; God may swear by any of creation, while people may swear only by God, supported by 70:40.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:56:71-75/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:56:71-75/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:56:71-75/r4.claim: The negating particle in the oath is extra; the “settings of the stars” are their setting places and western horizons.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:56:71-75/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:56:71-75/r5.speaker: قيل
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:56:71-75/r5.claim: Another interpretation takes the stars in the oath to mean the stars of the Qur'an.

JISHUMI:v9p6763#2/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v9p6763#2/r1.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
JISHUMI:v9p6763#2/r1.claim: They read mawqiʿ in the singular, intending the collective class of star-settings.

JISHUMI:v9p6763#2/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v9p6763#2/r2.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v9p6763#2/r2.claim: The remaining readers use the plural mawāqiʿ.

JISHUMI:v9p6763#2/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v9p6763#2/r3.speaker: عيسى بن عمرو
JISHUMI:v9p6763#2/r3.claim: Isa ibn Amr reads fa-la-uqsim with a clearly articulated oath form.

JISHUMI:v9p6763#2/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v9p6763#2/r4.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v9p6763#2/r4.claim: Qasam means an oath and derives from qasāma; mawqiʿ is the place where something falls or occurs.

JISHUMI:v9p6763#2/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v9p6763#2/r5.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v9p6763#2/r5.claim: Karīm describes something whose nature is to be honored; tanzīl is a verbal noun used by extension to describe what is revealed.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p22/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p22/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p22/r1.claim: Most exegetes take فلا أقسم as “I swear,” with لا extra; ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar reads فلأقسم with explicit hamza.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p22/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p22/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p22/r2.claim: Alternatively, لا rebuts the disbelievers’ claim that the Qur’an is magic, poetry, or soothsaying before beginning the oath.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p22/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p22/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p22/r3.claim: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read “position” singular; others read “positions” plural.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p22/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p22/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p22/r4.claim: The locations are the stars of Qur’anic revelation, since it descended in installments.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p22/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p22/r5.speaker: جماعة من المفسرين
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p22/r5.claim: The locations are star settings and places of descent; ʿAṭāʾ says their stations, and al-Ḥasan says their scattering at resurrection.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p466/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p466/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p466/r1.claim: In فَلَا أُقْسِمُ, the لا is an emphatic extra particle, so the phrase means ‘I swear,’ like the usage in 57:29.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p466/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p466/r2.speaker: الحسن
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p466/r2.claim: Al-Hasan reads فلأقسم, understood as ‘I indeed swear’: an initial lām governs an underlying أنا أقسم clause whose subject is omitted.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p466/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p466/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p466/r3.claim: The lām is not an oath particle: it lacks the normally required emphatic nūn, and an oath's response is future while the oath itself is present.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p466/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p466/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p466/r4.claim: The stars' settings may be a moment of special divine acts, angelic worship, night prayer, and descending mercy, explaining the oath's declared greatness.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p466/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p466/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p466/r5.claim: Alternatively, the stars' stations and courses display a measure of divine power and wisdom beyond description.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p466/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p466/r7.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p466/r7.claim: Another interpretation takes the stars' positions as the times when Qur'anic passages descended in installments.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p250#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p250#2/r1.speaker: بعض النحويين
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p250#2/r1.claim: Some grammarians call lā in fa-lā uqsim extra, yielding I swear; Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and others take it as negation before a new oath, and another group treats it as an emphatic oath opener.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p250#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p250#2/r2.speaker: الحسن والثقفي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p250#2/r2.claim: Al-Ḥasan and al-Thaqafī read fa-la-uqsim without the alif; Abū al-Fatḥ analyzes it as fa-la-anā aqsam.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p250#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p250#2/r3.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب وابن عباس وابن مسعود وأهل الكوفة وحمزة والكسائي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p250#2/r3.claim: Most read mawāqiʿ in the plural; these authorities read mawqiʿ in the singular with collective meaning, like referring to all donkey sounds as one sound-kind.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p250#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p250#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس وعكرمة ومجاهد وغيرهم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p250#2/r4.claim: They identify the stars as the stages of Quran revelation: the Quran descended at once to the lower heaven or the Frequented House, then in installments to Muhammad over twenty years.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p251/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p251/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p251/r1.claim: The Quran-revelation interpretation is supported by the following pronoun referring to the Quran, the only prior referent on that reading; others allow the pronoun to refer to the well-known Quran without explicit prior mention.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p251/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p251/r2.speaker: جمهور كثير من المفسرين
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p251/r2.claim: Many commentators instead identify the stars as celestial bodies: Mujāhid and Abū ʿUbayda say their settings and risings, Qatada their locations, others their falling at demons, and al-Ḥasan their scattering at Resurrection.

TABRISI:56:75/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:56:75/r1.speaker: أهل الكوفة غير عاصم
TABRISI:56:75/r1.claim: The Kufans other than Asim read the noun in the singular, while the remaining readers use the plural.

TABRISI:56:75/r12.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:56:75/r12.speaker: author
TABRISI:56:75/r12.claim: The oath means ‘I do swear’ in the present; Quranic oaths are present, whereas a future oath would require the emphatic nūn, so the negating particle is extra.

TABRISI:56:75/r13.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:56:75/r13.speaker: author
TABRISI:56:75/r13.claim: An oath is a clause that confirms a report by placing it among what is true rather than false.

TABRISI:56:75/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:56:75/r3.speaker: الحسن والثقفي
TABRISI:56:75/r3.claim: An anomalous reading has ‘so I swear’ without the alif.

TABRISI:56:75/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:56:75/r5.speaker: أبو عبيدة
TABRISI:56:75/r5.claim: He explains the oath as an actual oath and the stars' locations as their settings, where they disappear.

TABRISI:56:75/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:56:75/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:56:75/r6.claim: Another explanation makes the locations those of Quranic revelation as it descended to the Prophet in successive portions.

TABRISI:56:75/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:56:75/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:56:75/r7.claim: The plural can be used for a verbal noun because its instances differ; the singular is a generic noun.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r1.speaker: سعيد بن جبير، الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r1.claim: On this reading, lā is emphatic and the oath means simply I swear; al-Zajjāj gives a parallel phrase.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r10.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r10.claim: Alternatively, the stars are the portions of Qur'an, revealed in separate installments, and their locations are the places of revelation.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r2.speaker: الماوردي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r2.claim: Alternatively lā retains its basic negation, with an implied prohibition against denying the stated favors and proofs.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r3.speaker: علي بن أحمد النيسابوري
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r3.claim: Alternatively lā rejects the unbelievers' claims that the Qur'an is magic, poetry, or soothsaying, then a new oath begins.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r4.speaker: الحسن
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r4.claim: Ḥasan reads falāuqsim without an alif between the lām and hamza.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r5.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r5.claim: They read mawqiʿ, singular; Abū ʿAlī explains it as a generic noun, while the plural denotes the stars' differing locations.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r6.speaker: الجمهور
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r6.claim: The stars are the stars of the sky; one interpretation of their locations is their scattering at the Resurrection.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r7.speaker: الحسن
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r7.claim: The locations are where the stars collapse and scatter on the Day of Resurrection.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r8.speaker: عطاء وقتادة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r8.claim: The locations are the stars' stations or courses.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r9.speaker: أبو عبيدة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p150#2/r9.claim: The locations are where the stars set in the west.

RAZI-FULL:v29p162#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p162#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p162#2/r1.claim: After opponents exhaust their objections, they can say rhetorical force rather than the truth of the argument overcame them; God therefore teaches the Prophet to swear and affirm the truth.

RAZI-FULL:v29p162#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p162#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p162#2/r2.claim: The oath prefixed by bā follows proof that God creates and provides and possesses majesty; because they still disbelieved, only an oath remained to declare the Prophet truthful.

RAZI-FULL:v29p163#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p163#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p163#2/r1.claim: One view takes the stars' sites as their rising and settings, or their settings alone, where they fall.

RAZI-FULL:v29p163#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p163#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p163#2/r2.claim: A second view identifies the sites as the stars' positions in the sky among their signs and stations.

RAZI-FULL:v29p163#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p163#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p163#2/r3.claim: A third view refers to stars' positions when they pursue devils during their contest.

RAZI-FULL:v29p163#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p163#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p163#2/r4.claim: A fourth view refers to their positions at the Resurrection when the stars scatter.

RAZI-FULL:v29p163#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p163#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p163#2/r5.claim: For the Qurʾān's 'stars,' the sites may be the hearts of God's servants, angels, messengers, and righteous believers, or the Qurʾān's meanings and rulings.

RAZI-FULL:v29p163#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p163#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p163#2/r6.claim: The oath also points to divine choice: just as human creation, death, crops, and water show power over opposites, each star's assignment to one location among equivalent locations proves a freely choosing agent; these are cosmic signs alongside signs within people.

RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r1.claim: One transmitted analysis makes lā extra, as in 57:29, so the phrase means that he swears.

RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r2.claim: Another analysis derives lā from an emphatic lām whose fatḥa was lengthened, as at a pause.

RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r3.claim: A third analysis treats lā as negating the unbelievers claim, followed by an oath.

RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r4.claim: He also takes lā literally but as a rhetorical construction like refusing to describe an event too great to explain; the apparent prohibition conveys its magnitude.

RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r5.claim: One possible force is that the matter is too evident to require an oath; this works if the implied object is the Lord of created things.

RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r6.claim: Another possible force is emphatic escalation: not a thousand oaths or a prince head, but a sultan, because the sworn-by is greater.

RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p163/r7.claim: The escalation reading faces an objection: Qurʾānic oaths mention created things, not God or His attributes; the first reading avoids this if the Lord of those things is implied.

QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r1.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r1.claim: Most commentators treat lā as an extra particle, so the sense is an oath, confirmed by the following statement that it is a mighty oath.

QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r10.speaker: القشيري
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r10.claim: Al-Qushayrī says it is an oath: God may swear by whatever He wills, whereas people may swear only by God and His eternal attributes.

QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r11.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r11.claim: The reading fala-uqsim and God's other oaths by created things support treating it as an oath.

QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r12.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r12.claim: He interprets the star positions as the staged revelation of the Quran from the Preserved Tablet through the recording angels and Gabriel to Muhammad over twenty years.

QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r13.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r13.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās says the Quran descended to the lowest heaven all at once, then in installments of five verses or fewer or more; al-Anbārī transmits it without grading.

QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r14.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r14.speaker: ابن مسعود
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r14.claim: Ibn Masʿūd interprets the positions of the stars as the Quran's clear, decisive verses.

QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r15.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r15.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r15.claim: They read mawqiʿ in the singular, as do the other named readers; singular can be a generic noun, while plural marks differing kinds.

QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r2.speaker: الفراء
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r2.claim: Al-Farrāʾ takes lā as negation: the claim is false, and God then begins an oath; “No, by God” can reject a preceding assertion without negating the oath.

QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r3.claim: Another view makes lā an attention-getting particle like alā, drawing notice to the Quran's virtue and rejecting claims that it is poetry, magic, or soothsaying.

QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r4.speaker: الحسن وحميد وعيسى بن عمر
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r4.claim: They read fala-uqsima without an alif after the lām as a real present-tense verb with an implied subject; a future reading would normally require nūn.

QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r5.speaker: قتادة وغيره
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r5.claim: They identify the stars' positions as their places of setting.

QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r6.speaker: عطاء بن أبي رباح
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r6.claim: ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ says the positions are the stars' stations.

QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r7.speaker: الحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r7.claim: Al-Ḥasan interprets the positions as the stars' scattering at Resurrection.

QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r8.speaker: الضحاك
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r8.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says they are the anwaʾ, the star-settings to which pre-Islamic Arabs attributed rainfall.

QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r9.speaker: الماوردي
QURTUBI-FULL:56:75-77/r9.claim: Al-Māwardī says the phrase can be understood literally as a negation of an oath.

BAYDAWI-FULL:56:74-75/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:56:74-75/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:56:74-75/r2.claim: فلا أقسم can mean the matter is too clear to need an oath, an oath with emphatic extra لا, or أنا أقسم with an omitted subject; alternatively لا rejects a claim opposed to the oath’s object.

BAYDAWI-FULL:56:74-75/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:56:74-75/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:56:74-75/r3.claim: The stars’ مواقع are their settings, whose disappearance points to an enduring effective Creator, their stations and orbits, or the occasions when Qur’anic passages descended.

BAYDAWI-FULL:56:74-75/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:56:74-75/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:56:74-75/r4.claim: Hamza and al-Kisāʾī read the singular بموقع.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p211#7/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p211#7/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p211#7/r1.claim: “I swear” has an emphatic extra lā; another reading “I shall swear” uses an initial lām, not an oath lām, which should pair with an emphatic nūn.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p211#7/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p211#7/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p211#7/r2.claim: The phrase means the stars' settings; Ḥamza and ʿAlī have a singular “setting.”

NASAFI-FULL:v4p211#7/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p211#7/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p211#7/r3.claim: The settings may be special divine acts at night's end, angelic worship, or the night prayers and descent of mercy and pleasure, making the oath momentous.

QASHANI:56:73-82/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:56:73-82/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:56:73-82/r2.claim: The stars’ settings may mean times when the sanctified Muhammadan soul connects with the Holy Spirit and receives Qur’anic verses, luminous and noble connections.

QASHANI:56:73-82/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:56:73-82/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:56:73-82/r3.claim: Alternatively, star settings are moments when the Prophet’s senses vanish from bodily perception as his secret is absorbed in the unseen, holiness, and divine unity.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p90/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p90/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p90/r3.claim: One interpretation treats لا as an emphatic extra particle, making the phrase a direct oath; another understands a denial of the disbelievers' claim before beginning the oath, but Abū Ḥayyān rejects this because it requires deleting both parts of لا's clause without a question prompting it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p90/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p90/r4.speaker: سعيد بن جبير وبعض النحاة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p90/r4.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and some grammarians say the denied proposition is omitted before a fresh oath, but Abū Ḥayyān rules out this deletion without a prior question.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p90/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p90/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p90/r5.claim: A further account takes لا as a rhetorical opening that intensifies the oath, as in established speech patterns.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r1.claim: Abū Ḥayyān prefers reading the initial lām as lengthened by its fatḥa, yielding an alif and the sense ‘I swear.’

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r2.speaker: أبو الفتح
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r2.claim: Abū al-Fatḥ and al-Zamakhsharī construe al-Ḥasan’s reading with an omitted subject, ‘I do swear,’ since they deny swearing over a present-tense verb.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r3.speaker: ابن عصفور
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAṣfūr and others say an oath cannot be made over a present-tense verb, requiring the clause to be nominalized.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r4.claim: Abū Ḥayyān sides with grammarians who permit swearing over a present-tense verb and cites poetry using that construction.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r5.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r5.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī objects that al-Ḥasan’s lām lacks the expected emphatic nūn and makes a present-tense oath answer express the future.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r6.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says the missing nūn is disputed: Basrans require it, while Kufans prefer but permit its interchange with the lām.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r7.claim: He accepts the tense objection but treats it as support for an oath-lām: a present oath may answer another oath, while future oaths take nūn.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r8.claim: Most readers use plural mawāqiʿ; ʿUmar, ʿAbd Allāh, Ibn ʿAbbās, the Medinans, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī read singular mawqiʿ intended collectively.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p91/r9.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid, and others interpret the star positions as the successive descents of Qurʾānic revelation, supported by the next verse’s mention of the Qurʾān.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p92/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p92/r1.speaker: مجاهد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p92/r1.claim: Mujāhid and Abū ʿUbayda interpret the stars as celestial bodies at their risings and settings.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p92/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p92/r2.speaker: قتادة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p92/r2.claim: Qatāda says the star positions are their places in the sky.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p92/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p92/r3.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p92/r3.claim: Al-Ḥasan interprets the positions as where stars fall on the Day of Resurrection.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p92/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p92/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p92/r4.claim: Another interpretation places the stars at their dispersal after the ‘ʿafārī’; those taking them as celestial bodies let context explain the pronoun in ‘it is.’

SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r1.speaker: شاعر مجهول
SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r1.claim: Poems cited by the author illustrate the Kufan allowance for alternating oath lām and nūn.

SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r2.claim: A related passage at 4:65 has a different possible analysis; the author also points forward to Ibn Kathir's reading at 75:1.

SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r3.speaker: العامة
SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r3.claim: The common reading has plural مواقع; the two Kufan readers have singular موقع, which can stand for a plural because it is a verbal noun, meaning the stars' settings or courses.

SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r4.speaker: قيل
SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r4.claim: The stars' locations may mean their setting places, or their falling apart on the Day of Resurrection; another view identifies the stars with the Quran.

SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r5.claim: If the stars mean the Quran, the oath's answer is إنه لقرآن كريم, with وإنه لقسم interrupting the oath and لو تعلمون interrupting the adjective-noun relation.

SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r6.speaker: ابن عطية
SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r6.claim: Ibn Atiyya says وإنه لقسم emphasizes and draws attention to the sworn object, leaving only لو تعلمون as an interruption.

SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:56:75#2/r7.claim: The author replies that emphasis and drawing attention are exactly the purpose of a parenthetical interruption.

SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r1.speaker: جماعة من المفسرين والنحويين
SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r1.claim: One analysis makes فلا a negation whose omitted content is the disbeliever's claim having no proof, then begins an oath; critics say this deletes both noun and predicate of لا.

SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r2.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r2.claim: The Shaykh defends that analysis because it is attributed to Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Ibn Abbas's pupil, and is unlikely to be unsupported.

SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r3.speaker: قيل
SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r3.claim: A second analysis makes لا emphatic and effectively means فأقسم, as in لئلا يعلم and a poetic example.

SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r4.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r4.claim: The Shaykh proposes that فلا is an initial lām with a lengthened vowel, originally فلأقسم; the author calls this very weak.

SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r5.speaker: الحسن وعيسى
SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r5.claim: They read فلأقسم with one lām; the author gives either initial lām plus an omitted topic, or an oath lām governing a present verb as Kufans allow.

SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r6.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r6.claim: Al-Zamakhshari rejects an oath lām because it normally takes an emphatic nūn and because the oath verb should be present while the response is future.

SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:56:75/r7.claim: The author notes that the interchange of lām and nūn is a Basran constraint; Kufans permit it, so al-Zamakhshari's objection is not universal.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r1.claim: The Qur’an’s inimitability appears in the precise placement of every word and in the ordered links among clauses, verses, and stories.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r11.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r11.speaker: ابن برجان
BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r11.claim: Ibn Barjān says each setting star has a corresponding rising star, called its “watcher” by relation to the setting one.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r2.claim: Each passage functions as a cause, proof, or completion of what follows, making the composition coherent and compelling.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r3.claim: God sent the Prophet with guidance and truth, including decisive wisdom, heart-softening exhortation, and the best form of argument.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r4.claim: The opponents claim the Qur’an’s force comes from the Prophet’s debating skill rather than the truth of his proof, so they resort to accusing him of overpowering them.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r5.claim: Oaths multiply near the Qur’an’s end, especially in its final seven surahs, after decisive evidence has left opponents no other excuse.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r6.claim: In “lā uqsim,” lā either negates the opposite of the sworn truth or signals that the denied matter merits an even greater oath.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r7.claim: The “sites of the stars” refer both to the successive descents of illuminating Qur’anic passages and to the stars’ ordered settings, times, and places.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r8.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p423/r8.claim: Stars’ settings show power to fold creation and annihilate it, while their rising shows power to create after annihilation.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p424/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p424/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p424/r1.claim: The two easts and two wests include the sun, moon, stars, and twenty-eight lunar mansions; the moon passes one mansion each night.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p424/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p424/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p424/r2.claim: The moon completes its circuit through the mansions in a month; the sun remains in each for fourteen days, and its setting is paired with the next mansion’s rising.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p424/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p424/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p424/r3.claim: The world’s rainfall, seasonal moderation, and distribution of provisions display beneficent divine ordering.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p424/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p424/r4.speaker: أبو الحكم
BIQAI-FULL:v7p424/r4.claim: Abū al-Ḥakam elaborates the blessings of rainfall: it softens severe cold, tempers scorching heat, and completes the earth’s yearly cycle.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p424/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p424/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p424/r5.claim: The seasons complete the earth’s blessings and the apportionment of its provisions over four days; his reading has fīhā instead of bihā in 41:10.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p424/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p424/r6.speaker: أبو الحكم
BIQAI-FULL:v7p424/r6.claim: Abū al-Ḥakam calls the world, in this comparison, a lesser paradise; its corresponding severe heat and cold would be a lesser hell.

DURR-FULL:v8p25/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r1.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r1.claim: Mujahid gives an interpretation rendered in the source as al-jimāʿ, a gathering or conjunction.

DURR-FULL:v8p25/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r10.claim: Ibn Abbas says the Quran descended to the lowest heaven together, then reached earth in groups of three, five, or varying numbers of verses.

DURR-FULL:v8p25/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r11.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r11.claim: Ibn Masud's reading takes the oath as by the decisive parts of the Quran sent down successively.

DURR-FULL:v8p25/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r2.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r2.claim: Mujahid also interprets the locations as the stars of the sky.

DURR-FULL:v8p25/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r3.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r3.claim: Qatada says the oath is by the places where stars set or fall.

DURR-FULL:v8p25/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r4.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r4.claim: Hasan interprets the stars' locations as their scattering and falling apart on the Resurrection Day.

DURR-FULL:v8p25/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r5.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r5.claim: Hasan also glosses the locations as where stars disappear.

DURR-FULL:v8p25/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r6.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r6.claim: Qatada interprets the locations as the stars' stations or courses.

DURR-FULL:v8p25/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies both the star locations and the tremendous oath as the Quran.

DURR-FULL:v8p25/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r8.claim: Ibn Abbas says the Quran descended all at once on Laylat al-Qadr from the highest heaven to the lowest, then came down over the years in installments.

DURR-FULL:v8p25/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p25/r9.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas associates the sites with the Quran's successive stars of revelation.

DURR-FULL:v8p26/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p26/r1.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v8p26/r1.claim: Mujahid interprets the stars' locations as the decisive Quran.

DURR-FULL:v8p26/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p26/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p26/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas says the sites are the repository of the Book, from its beginning to its end.

BURSEVI:v9p274/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p274/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p274/r5.claim: ‘Nay, I swear’ means ‘I swear’; the extra la emphasizes the statement, while the contrary reading fails because the object of this magnificent oath is specified.

BURSEVI:v9p274/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p274/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p274/r6.claim: The sites of stars are their settings; their disappearance points to a lasting, unchanging agent, or marks the night worshippers’ hour when mercy descends, or means their stations and orbits displaying power and wisdom.

BURSEVI:v9p274/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p274/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
BURSEVI:v9p274/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets the stars as the Qur’an and their locations as the times of its revelation.

BURSEVI:v9p274/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p274/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p274/r8.claim: Another interpretation makes the stars the Companions and later guiding scholars, with their locations being their graves.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r1.speaker: قتادة، الحسن
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r1.claim: Qatāda and al-Ḥasan take the sites of the stars as their settings, since their disappearance points to an enduring, unchanging Agent and the time is associated with worship and mercy.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r10.speaker: ابن عباس، أهل المدينة، حمزة، الكسائي
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r10.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, the Medinans, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī read the singular mawqiʿ, intended collectively.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r2.speaker: أبو هريرة
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r2.claim: Al-Bukhārī and Muslim transmit a raised report from Abū Hurayra that God descends in the last third of the night and calls people to pray, ask, and seek forgiveness.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r3.speaker: الحسن
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r3.claim: A second report from al-Ḥasan takes the sites as the stars' scattering on the Resurrection; their fall need not occur all at once and displays divine majesty while confirming resurrection.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r4.speaker: أبو جعفر، أبو عبد الله
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r4.claim: Abū Jaʿfar and Abū ʿAbd Allāh, from their forefathers, identify the sites as where stars fall after jinn eavesdroppers are pursued.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r5.claim: Another view means the lunar mansions that pre-Islamic Arabs believed caused rain; the occasion report is not decisive, since ordinary settings could also be intended.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r6.speaker: قتادة
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r6.claim: Qatāda, in reports from ʿAbd al-Razzāq and Ibn Jarīr, says the sites are the stars' stations and paths, with “falling” meaning descent, a sign of God's immense power and wisdom.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and others say the sites are the occasions of Qurʾānic revelation; reports say it descended all at once to the lowest heaven, then in installments over years.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r8.claim: Al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ḥākim (who authenticates it), and al-Bayhaqī transmit Ibn ʿAbbās's account of the Qurʾān's descent in one night and later installments.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152#2/r9.claim: The revelation reading gives the next verse's pronoun an evident antecedent and needs no contextual inference; its rationale is especially clear.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r1.claim: The prefixed lā may be an emphatic extra particle, as in the Qurʾānic example lā-yaʿlama ahlu al-kitāb.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r10.speaker: أبو مسلم وجمع
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r10.claim: Abū Muslim and others take the words literally: no oath is needed because the matter is too clear, much less this great oath; al-Ālūsī rejects the Rūmī muftī's objection as inattentive.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r2.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r2.claim: Abū Ḥayyān chooses to treat lā as an oath-lām whose vowel is lengthened into an alif, adducing a rare analogous spelling and a Qurʾānic reading.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r3.speaker: الحسن، عيسى
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r3.claim: Al-Ḥasan and ʿĪsā read falā qasam, supporting the analysis that the following clause is a present-tense oath.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r4.claim: This analysis assumes a present-tense verb can be sworn by; the cited grammarians permit that, whereas Ibn ʿAṣfūr and the Basrans say a present verb takes an oath only when intended as future and then requires the emphatic nūn.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r5.speaker: ابن عصفور، البصريون
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r5.claim: Ibn ʿAṣfūr and Basran grammarians reject swearing by a present-tense verb; when future meaning is intended they require emphatic nūn, making its omission very weak.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r6.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r6.claim: Abū Ḥayyān parses the readings with an omitted subject and initial lām, roughly “for I indeed swear,” though the author objects that omitting the emphasized subject is awkward.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r7.speaker: سعيد بن جبير وبعض النحاة
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r7.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and some grammarians take lā as denying unbelievers' claims that the Qurʾān is sorcery, poetry, or soothsaying, then begin a new oath.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r8.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r8.claim: Abū Ḥayyān objects to the denial reading because it requires deleting both the subject and predicate of lā outside a question-answer construction.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r9.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v27p152/r9.claim: Another view treats lā before an oath as an opening formula, as in the cited line addressed to Ibnat al-ʿĀmirī.

ELMALILI:56:75-96#2/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:56:75-96#2/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:56:75-96#2/r1.claim: Commentators explain the negative particle in ‘fa-lā uqsimu’ as an extra rhythmic particle, an emphatic lām with an expanded vowel, or genuine negation; the author prefers genuine negation.

ELMALILI:56:75-96#2/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:56:75-96#2/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:56:75-96#2/r2.claim: God reinforces revealed signs and proofs with many oaths, especially in early and final-period surahs, because people who cannot debate may claim truth while blaming their opponent for unfairness.

ELMALILI:56:75-96#2/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:56:75-96#2/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:56:75-96#2/r3.claim: On the preferred reading the oath means ‘No, the matter is not as they think; I swear’, or that no further argument is needed before swearing.

ELMALILI:56:75-96#2/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:56:75-96#2/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:56:75-96#2/r4.claim: Possible literal referents of the stars’ stations include their setting or rising places, celestial positions and mansions, meteor-fall locations, or where stars fall at the Resurrection.

ELMALILI:56:75-96#2/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:56:75-96#2/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:56:75-96#2/r5.claim: The more fitting sense is the successive portions of the Qur’an revealed at each descent; this allusion is intended at least by double entendre, so ‘stars’ should not be translated literally.

ELMALILI:56:75-96#2/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:56:75-96#2/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:56:75-96#2/r6.claim: On the Qur’anic sense, the stations may encompass angels, the Prophet, memorizer-hearts, written pages, meanings, and the occasions or rulings prompting revelation.

ELMALILI:56:75-96/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:56:75-96/r1.speaker: رازي
ELMALILI:56:75-96/r1.claim: Al-Rāzī links the opening particle to what precedes: God equipped the Messenger with proof, wisdom, good exhortation, and argument, yet the disbelievers still refused faith.

ELMALILI:56:75-96/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:56:75-96/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:56:75-96/r2.claim: A debater’s apparent win need not prove his claim true; it may reflect intellectual strength and skill in assembling arguments.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p330/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p330/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p330/r1.claim: “No, I swear” can mean “I swear,” with extra la emphasizing caution against a false oath; alternatively it signals that the truth is so evident no oath is needed, a usage that became emphatic assertion.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p330/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p330/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p330/r2.claim: The author prefers the no-need-for-an-oath sense as better matching Quranic parallels; either reading draws attention to the worthiness of the sworn subject.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p330/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p330/r4.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p330/r4.claim: Saʿid b. Jubayr and some exegetes treat la as an independent reply to denials that the Quran is poetry, magic, ancient tales, or a soothsayer’s speech; “I swear” then begins a new statement.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p330/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p330/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p330/r5.claim: On that reading, the oath follows the signs that establish resurrection and refutes the opponents’ claims about the Quran.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p330/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p330/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p330/r6.claim: Mawaqiʿ can mean places where fixed and wandering stars fall or set; their ordered motions and alternation display a wondrous system and the Creator’s greatness.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p331/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p331/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p331/r1.claim: Wuquʿ can also mean settling in a place, so star sites may be their locations and courses, like the sky’s constellations.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p331/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p331/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p331/r2.claim: The sites are the stars’ precisely regulated orbits, constellations, and lunar mansions.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p331/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p331/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p331/r3.claim: Either interpretation honors the stars because their courses reveal divine wisdom and power.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p331/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p331/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p331/r4.claim: Mawaqiʿ may be the plural of the mimetic verbal noun for occurrence.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p331/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p331/r5.speaker: ابن عباس وعكرمة
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p331/r5.claim: Some exegetes read najm as a portion or installment and take the “stars” as successive portions of Quranic revelation, making the oath directly about the Quran.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p332/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p332/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p332/r2.claim: Most read mawāqiʿ in the plural; Hamza, al-Kisaʾi, and Khalaf read singular mawqiʿ, a mimetic noun for setting or its place.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p332/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p332/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p332/r3.claim: The singular reading can mean the stars’ setting, comparable to the Lord of east and west.

TABATABAI:56:57-96#2/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:56:57-96#2/r6.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
TABATABAI:56:57-96#2/r6.claim: After rain, some people thanked God for mercy while others credited a star's setting; Ibn Abbas reports that these verses were revealed on that occasion.

TABATABAI:56:57-96#2/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:56:57-96#2/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:56:57-96#2/r7.claim: Sunni reports widely place the revelation in Medina, but that dating does not fit the surah's context.

TABATABAI:56:75-80/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:56:75-80/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:56:75-80/r1.claim: The phrase is an oath; one reading treats lā as extra and another as a negation accompanying the oath.

TABATABAI:56:75-80/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:56:75-80/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:56:75-80/r2.claim: Mawāqiʿ most naturally means the places or stations of the stars in the sky.

TABATABAI:56:75-80/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:56:75-80/r3.speaker: بعضهم
TABATABAI:56:75-80/r3.claim: Some take mawāqiʿ as a verbal noun meaning the falling of stars at the Resurrection or of shooting stars upon devils.

TABATABAI:56:75-80/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:56:75-80/r4.speaker: بعضهم
TABATABAI:56:75-80/r4.claim: Another explanation is the places where stars set.

ASAD-NOTES:56:75#n26/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:56:75#n26/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:56:75#n26/r1.claim: Mawqi can mean the time, place, or manner at which something comes down; Asad also renders the phrase as the stars' setting or orbiting.

ASAD-NOTES:56:75#n26/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:56:75#n26/r2.speaker: commentators
ASAD-NOTES:56:75#n26/r2.claim: Many commentators take the phrase to refer to the stars breaking apart at the Last Hour.

ASAD-NOTES:56:75#n26/r3.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:56:75#n26/r3.speaker: Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and As-Suddi
ASAD-NOTES:56:75#n26/r3.claim: They interpret the phrase as the Qur'an's gradual, step-by-step revelation, a reading supported by the following verses.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p135/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p135/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p135/r1.claim: This is the seventh and final Makkan sūrah in its group, closing the Makkan portion.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p135/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p135/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p135/r2.claim: The sūrah sums up the reward-and-punishment discussion from Qāf through al-Raḥmān, replacing prior detailed arguments with the certain outcome.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p135/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p135/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p135/r3.claim: Earlier sūrahs grounded the case in reason, human nature, and evidence from the inner and outer worlds.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p136/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p136/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p136/r2.claim: Verses 75–96 signal the Qur’an’s exalted status and its protection from Satan and his agents.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p136/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p136/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p136/r3.claim: Quraysh are cautioned not to ignore the sublime message and thereby bring doom upon themselves.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p157/r6.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p157/r6.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p157/r6.claim: Section III closes the sūrah by affirming the Qur'an's reality and divine, protected transmission, calling it guidance and spiritual food, and warning Quraysh that rejecting it cannot save them from God's coming judgment.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p158/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p158/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p158/r1.claim: The particle lā is separate from uqsimu; before the oath's affirmation, it negates the addressee's false view, a familiar Arabic and Qur'anic usage.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p158/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p158/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p158/r2.claim: Islahi illustrates the construction with 4:65: verbal profession alone does not make hypocrites true believers, who must accept the Prophet's arbitration.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p159/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p159/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p159/r1.claim: The opening la refutes the claim that the Qur’an is soothsayer nonsense before affirming its truth; this abrupt denial is a natural, forceful rhetorical style.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p159/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p159/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p159/r2.claim: La should not be treated as superfluous: eloquent discourse has no superfluous words, and dismissing it without principle risks opening forbidden matters; Islahi will explain its Arabic usage at 57:29.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p159/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p159/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p159/r3.claim: Mawqiʿ means a place where something happens or falls; here the plural denotes the heavenly stations where jinn ambush divine secrets and are struck by meteors.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p159/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p159/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p159/r4.claim: At the Qur’an’s revelation God specially protected revelation from jinn eavesdroppers, who acknowledged that the sky’s stations were guarded by meteors.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p160/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p160/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p160/r1.claim: The jinn’s mawāqiʿ are their ambush stations, while this verse’s mawāqiʿ are the targets of the shooting stars; al-nujūm here means shooting stars.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p160/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p160/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p160/r2.claim: The Qur’an elsewhere calls these meteors a bombardment against devils, and related explanations occur at 53:1–5 and 55:35.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:56:75/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:56:75/r1.speaker: Müfessirler
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:56:75/r1.claim: The “positions of stars” are commonly taken as their rising or setting places and orbital stations, especially where stars fall at the Resurrection.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:56:75/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:56:75/r2.speaker: Bazı ilk dönem müfessirleri
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:56:75/r2.claim: Early exegetes also take the phrase as the Qur'an's gradual descent or portions, its clear verses, or the coherence between its beginning and end.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:56:75/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:56:75/r3.speaker: Râzî
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:56:75/r3.claim: He also suggests that the phrase may mean the hearts into which the Qur'an enters.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:56:75/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:56:75/r4.speaker: Günümüzdeki bazı Kur’an araştırmacıları
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:56:75/r4.claim: Some contemporary researchers associate the wording with hypothetical black holes or gas-cloud formations between stars.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:56:75/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:56:75/r5.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:56:75/r5.claim: The discussion of the oath points readers to the broader Qur'anic treatment of divine oaths.

QIRAAT-ER:56:75:5#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:56:75:5#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:56:75:5#1/r1.claim: The singular mawqiʿ replaces plural mawāqiʿ, changing multiple dispersed positions to a unified locus.

STUDYQURAN:56:75/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:56:75/r1.speaker: most commentators
STUDYQURAN:56:75/r1.claim: Most take the particle la in fa-la uqsimu as emphatic, rendering the oath “I swear.”

STUDYQURAN:56:75/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:56:75/r2.speaker: Q, Sh, Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:56:75/r2.claim: Some read la as negation: “Nay, I swear,” denouncing what opponents say before swearing.

STUDYQURAN:56:75/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:56:75/r3.speaker: R, Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:56:75/r3.claim: The places where stars descend most likely means when, where, or how celestial bodies set, or their stations, as in other Quranic references.

STUDYQURAN:56:75/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:56:75/r4.speaker: R, Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:56:75/r4.claim: Alternatively, the phrase may refer to stars fading on Judgment Day.

STUDYQURAN:56:75/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:56:75/r5.speaker: Aj
STUDYQURAN:56:75/r5.claim: If it refers to stars setting, the oath alludes to night hours considered especially good for voluntary devotions.

STUDYQURAN:56:75/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:56:75/r6.speaker: IK, Q, Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:56:75/r6.claim: Nujum can mean portions or installments, so the oath may refer to the Quran's gradual revelation in groups of three, four, or five verses over twenty-three years.

STUDYQURAN:56:75/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:56:75/r7.speaker: R
STUDYQURAN:56:75/r7.claim: The descending stars or Quranic installments may allude to their descent into the hearts of God's servants, angels, messengers, and righteous believers.

STUDYQURAN:56:intro/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:56:intro/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:56:intro/r5.claim: Five overlapping sections cover Judgment's signs, the three groups' destinies, proofs of resurrection, the revelation, and death and the Afterlife.
